design.hypothesis: After the receiver-lock change, small-file fresh copies are limited by per-file work on the receiving Mac. If so, -j8 and -j16 give little over -j4 while peer CPU rises, and the effect is stronger on pull (mars>mac), where small-deep takes about twice as long as push. --no-atomic at -j8 beats -j8 if temp-file rename costs matter. A large gap between durable_s and wall_s would point at writeback. This run leaves out the local tar-extraction baseline on the receiver and any sample/perf profile, so it bounds the limit by scaling and CPU, not by an absolute ceiling or a per-function breakdown.

analysis.summary: Re-measuring no-op re-syncs (B1) showed xs-rs ahead of rsync both ways. At -j4 it took 0.269 to 0.308 of rsync's time on real-congress and 0.231 on real-psample push. At -j8 it was ahead in every cell, though psample pull at -j4 was too noisy to call (0.6, interval 0.213 to 1.689). The no-op question is closed, and next the lab races small-file fresh copies across -j1 to -j16 and --no-atomic (A2) to find which receiver-side limit to build against.

priorities.brief: No code. Race small-deep and small-flat fresh copies, push and pull, with xs-rs at -j1, -j4 (control), -j8 and -j16, plus -j8 with --no-atomic, and rsync -a for reference. The run shows four things. First, whether more receiving workers still help after the receiver-lock change (A1: 'fresh 0.411 (faster)'), which A1's pooled verdicts did not separate. Second, whether atomic temp-file-and-rename costs measurable time per file on the macOS receiver. Third, whether the push/pull asymmetry seen in lab races persists across job counts (small-deep 9.84 s push vs 19.878 s pull). Fourth, how client and peer CPU and RSS scale with -j, to show which end saturates. If -j8 and -j16 stop improving while peer CPU keeps rising, the limit is receiver-side per-file work; that points at A3, A5 or A6. If --no-atomic helps clearly, the rename/fsync path is the limit (A7). Compare durable_s with wall_s to see how much time is spent after the copy reaching durability, which bears on writeback (A7). The lab cannot run local tar extraction or sample/perf, so the 'distance from local creation' baseline and the in-process profile are left out.
priorities.why: It is the only buildable node. It decides which of A3, A5, A6 or A7 to build next on the small-file fresh copies, where xs-rs spends the most per-file time on this link. Pull (mars>mac) is twice as slow as push on small-deep, and rsync takes 26.643 s and 48.05 s there. With B1 showing no-op re-syncs already ahead of rsync, small fresh copies are where the next gain is.

decision.reason: The run's status is 'failed' and it carries no lab verdicts, so this branch rests on the arm-vs-control effects alone. Some cells kept only 8 or 9 of 10 blocks. Even so, the hypothesis that xs-rs still trails rsync on no-op re-syncs is refuted. At the default -j4, xs-rs against rsync was 0.269 (0.235 to 0.309, 10 blocks) on congress push and 0.308 (0.262 to 0.361, 10 blocks) on congress pull. It was 0.231 (0.219 to 0.245, 8 blocks) on psample push. The one weak cell is psample pull at -j4: 0.6 with a 95% interval of 0.213 to 1.689 over 9 blocks, too wide to call, at 45.418 s against 75.716 s. At -j8 xs-rs is clearly ahead in all four cells: 0.249, 0.268, 0.185, and 0.191 (0.147 to 0.249) on psample pull. -j1 is also ahead everywhere it is decided: 0.519, 0.584 and 0.421, with psample pull at 0.82 (0.317 to 2.121), inconclusive. Going from -j1 to -j8 roughly halves time on every cell, so no serial bottleneck dominates. xs-rs CPU seconds are close to rsync's at -j4 (7.747 vs 8.098 on congress push), not far above. The lab records only total CPU, not a user/kernel split, so branches 0 and 1 could not be told apart anyway, and neither is needed: xs-rs is at or ahead of rsync both ways. The remaining oddity is the high variance of psample pull at -j4 (and xs-cpp-j4 there at 2.002, 0.912 to 4.393). That is noise worth watching, not a deficit against rsync. A measurement changes no code, so keep is false.

only fewer bytes: The compression change (c9e8d5d5f87d against 0a4953bec5d8) did not make copies faster on this link. Fresh copies were 'fresh 1.001 (equivalent)', 95% interval 0.974 to 1.030 over 8 blocks, at 12.42 s against 12.402 s. No-op re-syncs were 'noop 0.991 (inconclusive)', interval 0.942 to 1.043 over 8 blocks, at 1.714 s against 1.73 s. Eight blocks is the minimum. The fresh interval is reasonably tight around 1, but the no-op interval is wide, so this is weak evidence in both directions. The race also ran on mac-mars-usb10g, not on lab2's internet link, so it says nothing for or against the 'faster on lab2' branch. On the 10 GbE cable, where negative levels were meant to help, it bought no time. No later node depends on it. Drop it from the chain; the dictionary and long-range ideas would need a separate slow-link race.
